paras: The attempted lynchings of Percy Thompson and Ludie Martin were attempts in the summer of 1920 by mobs of white men to force the Lauderdale County jail at Meridian, Mississippi, and seize two Black prisoners. Officers turned back the mob that came for Thompson, who was later convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. The attempts drew notice chiefly through a new circuit judge's charge to the grand jury, reported under the headline "Grand Jury Told to Go After Mob."

Thompson was held on a charge of attempted criminal assault on "a young Syrian girl" in Meridian. Martin had been arrested as a suspect in the death of Carrie Hatcher, the 18-year-old daughter of George W. Hatcher, who had been choked to death near her home and her body left in a brook. The same months brought the murders of a suburban merchant and a night watchman, for which two Black men were held at Jackson "for fear that they might be lynched," and the lynching of James Spencer, a Black postal clerk, by masked men.

According to Judge C. C. Miller, "mobs of unmasked white men" had recently tried "to force the county jail" to get possession of Thompson and Martin. The attempts took place after the February criminal term and before August 1; no paper gave their dates, the size of the mobs or their leaders. In the Thompson case, a Meridian report said the mob was "only prevented" from taking him by "the strong stand" of the sheriff, the chief of police and their deputies. No account of the attempt on Martin beyond its mention was found.

Judge Miller opened the criminal term on August 2 and specially charged the grand jury on the attempts, asking it "to bring the guilty parties to justice." No report of indictments or arrests of mob members appears in the coverage, and the term adjourned on August 13 after about seventy-eight cases.

Thompson was tried in the circuit court, where the girl testified through an interpreter because she could not speak English. The jury found him guilty, and Judge Miller sentenced him to a life term in the penitentiary. Martin's fate is not reported.

The coverage found was entirely in white newspapers and came from Meridian correspondents writing about the court term rather than about the mobs themselves. A Meridian preview dated August 1 ran in the Birmingham Age-Herald and, nearly word for word, in the Brookhaven Semi-Weekly Leader, listing "two attempted lynchings" alongside "three of the foulest murders" in the county. The Memphis News Scimitar printed a one-sentence item naming Thompson and Martin as "a negro" and "a negro suspect," and a separate Meridian story that mentioned the attempted lynchings without names.

Only the Age-Herald gave the judge's charge prominence, quoting his reference to the "reckless disregard of the law by mobs." Its later trial report praised the officers' stand but called Thompson "the black" and described the attack on the girl as fact. No Black-press report of either attempt was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynchings of Percy Thompson and Ludie Martin
bases: Mobs of white men tried to force the county jail to seize two Black prisoners and were stopped, which the papers called attempted lynchings (A1, A2, A6).
No one was killed: Thompson was tried and sentenced (A6, A7) and no death of Martin is reported; the episode is an attempted lynching by mobs acting on criminal accusations (A2).

Two separate Meridian specials in the Age-Herald and the Memphis News Scimitar report the two attempted lynchings (A1, A4, A5), and the judge's charge and trial report describe the mob attempts (A2, A6), though most detail comes from one correspondent.

accounts.label: Report of Thompson's trial

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined the judge's charge 'GRAND JURY TOLD TO GO AFTER MOB' and quoted his reference to the 'reckless disregard of the law by mobs'.
The previews and the Memphis brief treated the attempts as docket items beside murders and the Spencer lynching, calling Thompson 'a negro' and giving the charges against both men.
The trial report credited officers' 'strong stand' against the mob while calling Thompson 'the black' and stating the attack as fact.
